q: The morning forecast says 'northerly, Force 5'. Which way is the wind blowing?
a: From the north, towards the south
o: From the south, towards the north
From the sea, towards the north
From the west, turning north later
why: Wind is always named by the direction it blows from.

q: The forecast for your day sail is Force 4. What kind of day is that for a yacht?
a: A moderate breeze, 11–16 knots — good sailing
o: Near calm — expect to motor most of the day
A gale, 34–40 knots — stay in harbour
A strong breeze, 22–27 knots — reefs needed
why: Force 4 is a moderate breeze, 11–16 knots, small waves with some white horses.

q: The afternoon forecast is north-west Force 6, and your crossing is 18 miles of open water. What does this mean for you as crew?
a: Strong wind — expect reefs, spray and a lively ride
o: Light airs — expect to motor most of the way
Moderate breeze — full sail and a gentle ride
Storm force — no yacht could put to sea
why: Force 6 is a strong breeze, 22–27 knots: reefs, rough water and lifejackets on.

q: The skipper decides to stay in port because the forecast is Force 8. What does that mean?
a: A gale, about 34–40 knots
o: A fresh breeze, about 17–21 knots
A light breeze, about 4–6 knots
A moderate breeze, about 11–16 knots
why: Force 8 is a gale — too much for a charter yacht and her crew.

q: What wind do you expect by mid-afternoon?
a: A breeze blowing in from the sea onto the land
o: A breeze blowing off the land out to sea
Flat calm until sunset
A wind that dies away by noon
why: Land heats faster than sea; the air over it rises and a sea breeze blows in by the afternoon.

fig.title: Hot summer day, Saronic Gulf
lines: The land is heating up fast

q: You are on anchor watch at 02:00 in a calm bay below hills. A light breeze springs up. Where does it most likely come from?
a: Off the land, blowing out to sea
o: Off the sea, blowing onto the land
Along the shore, from the east
Any side — night winds are random
why: At night the land cools faster than the sea, so a light land breeze blows offshore.

q: You are sailing in the Cyclades in August. From which direction does the Meltemi usually blow?
a: From the north, strongest in the afternoon
o: From the south, strongest at night
From the east, only in early spring
From the west, only after rain
why: The Meltemi is the Aegean's summer north wind, usually at its strongest in the afternoon.

q: Your next hop is 20 miles north across open water, and the Meltemi is forecast at Force 6–7 for three days. When is the crossing likely to be easiest?
a: Leave early, around dawn
o: Leave at noon, when it is warm
Leave mid-afternoon, after lunch
Any time — the Meltemi is steady
why: The Meltemi often eases overnight and builds through the day — cross early.

q: Close under the cliffs the water looks calm. What do you expect there?
a: Sudden strong gusts falling off the cliffs
o: A steady light breeze — it is sheltered
Flat calm — a safe place to drift
A steady wind, just like offshore
why: Wind spilling over high land drops down the lee side in violent gusts.

q: You are about to sail through the gap at A. What do you expect?
a: Stronger wind, squeezed through the gap
o: Lighter wind, sheltered by both islands
The wind swinging round to the south
No change from the open sea
why: Wind funnels between islands and round headlands — expect it to be stronger there.

q: You are keeping the barometer log. What do you tell the skipper?
a: It is falling fast — strong wind may be on the way
o: It is steady — settled weather ahead
It is rising — the wind should ease
Pressure means little in summer
why: A fall of several hPa in three hours is a warning that strong wind is coming.

q: What is most likely on the way?
a: A thunderstorm with sudden violent gusts
o: A steady sea breeze, slowly building
Fog rolling in from the open sea
A long spell of settled calm weather
why: Towering clouds with anvil tops are thunderstorm clouds: squalls, lightning and heavy rain.

fig.title: Afternoon, near the coast
lines: Hot and sticky since the morning
Tall cauliflower clouds over the hills
Tops spreading out flat, like an anvil

q: The skipper asks what to get ready. What do you suggest?
a: Reduce sail now and put lifejackets on
o: Keep full sail and try to outrun it
Wait for the first gust, then reef
Go below and leave the sails as they are
why: Reef before a squall arrives — its first gust can be far stronger than the wind ahead of it.

fig.title: Squall line ahead
lines: Dark wall of cloud, rain below it
Dark ruffled water coming your way

q: What does the visibility part of this forecast warn you about?
a: In places you may see less than 1 km
o: Visibility will stay over 10 miles
Fog only over land, not at sea
Rain, with good visibility in between
why: In forecasts 'fog' means visibility under 1000 m; 'poor' means under 2 miles.

fig.title: Coastal forecast
lines: Visibility: moderate, poor in fog patches

q: What will the afternoon be like?
a: A stronger north-westerly and a rougher sea
o: A south-easterly wind, easing later
Lighter wind and a calming sea
Rain showers and poor visibility
why: 'Increasing 6 later' and 'becoming rough': more wind and bigger waves as the day goes on.

q: What will this leg be like?
a: Upwind into wind and waves — slow and wet
o: Downwind with the wind behind — easy
Wind on the beam — fast and comfortable
Calm — you will motor all the way
why: A north-easterly course into a north wind is close-hauled, at the windiest time of day.

q: If the boat is still here at 15:00, which way is it being pushed?
a: Towards the beach — the sea breeze blows onshore
o: Away from the beach — a land breeze blows out
Nowhere — it will stay calm all day
Along the beach — a westerly sets in
why: The afternoon sea breeze blows onshore — off a south-facing beach it comes from the south.

fig.title: Lunch stop
lines: Anchored close off a south-facing beach

q: What do these signs together suggest?
a: A depression with strong wind is approaching
o: A settled high is building over you
A local sea breeze is about to start
Only a light shower, then sunshine
why: Fast-falling pressure, thickening high cloud and a new swell all point to an approaching low.

fig.title: Watch log
lines: High wispy cloud thickening from the west
A long swell starting to arrive

q: In the marina, the flag on the harbour office streams out towards the south-east. What wind is blowing?
a: A north-westerly
o: A south-easterly
A south-westerly
A north-easterly
why: A flag streams downwind, so the wind comes from the opposite side — the north-west.

q: Which Force on the Beaufort scale is this?
a: Force 6
o: Force 4
Force 5
Force 8
why: Force 6 is 22–27 knots, a strong breeze.
